(a) In General.—Section 1886(d)(5)(F)(vi) of the Social Security Act (42 U.S.C. 1395ww(d)(5)(F)(vi)) is amended by adding after and below subclause (II) the following:“In determining under subclause (II) the number of the hospital’s patient days for such period which consist of patients who (for such days) were eligible for medical assistance under a State plan approved under title XIX, the Secretary may, to the extent and for the period the Secretary determines appropriate, include patient days of patients not so eligible but who are regarded as such because they receive benefits under a demonstration project approved under title XI.”. 
    (b) Ratification and Prospective Application of Previous Regulations.—
        (1) In general.—Subject to paragraph (2), regulations described in paragraph (3), insofar as such regulations provide for the treatment of individuals eligible for medical assistance under a demonstration project approved under title XI of the Social Security Act under section 1886(d)(5)(F)(vi) of such Act, are hereby ratified, effective as of the date of their respective promulgations. 
        (2) No application to closed cost reports.—Paragraph (1) shall not be applied in a manner that requires the reopening of any cost reports which are closed as of the date of the enactment of this Act. 
        (3) Regulations described.—For purposes of paragraph (1), the regulations described in this paragraph are as follows:
            (A) 2000 regulation.—Regulations promulgated on January  20, 2000, at 65 Federal Register 3136 et seq., including the policy in such regulations regarding discharges occurring prior to January 20, 2000. 
            (B) 2003 regulation.—Regulations promulgated on August 1, 2003, at 68 Federal Register 45345 et seq.

fable.w: The tempting reading is that the references to regulations signal rulemaking and therefore public comment. But the section only has Congress ratify regulations already promulgated in 2000 and 2003, which is a past action confirmed inside the federal government, not a new rulemaking or comment process. The new discretion given to the Secretary to count demonstration-project patient days does not require regulation, consultation, a hearing, or any other involvement of outside parties, and the section grants no right to sue.
fable.s: are hereby ratified, effective as of the date of their respective promulgations

opus.w: Subsection (b) ratifies regulations that were already issued in 2000 and 2003. It does not require or authorize any new rulemaking, comment period or consultation, and past processes do not count as participation (see Example 5). Subsection (a) lets the Secretary decide on his own, 'to the extent... the Secretary determines appropriate,' with no requirement to act by regulation and no outside party involved. Seeing the word 'regulations' and reading it as granted rulemaking authority is therefore wrong.
opus.s: regulations described in paragraph (3), insofar as such regulations provide for the treatment of individuals eligible for medical assistance under a demonstration project approved under title XI of the Social Security Act under section 1886(d)(5)(F)(vi) of such Act, are hereby ratified, effective as of the date of their respective promulgations.
opus.b:
Answer: No. The tempting reading is "Yes," because subsection (b) refers to "regulations," and the examples count a grant of rulemaking authority as participation. That reading fails here.

- **Subsection (b) looks backward.** It ratifies regulations already issued in 2000 and 2003. It neither requires nor authorizes any new rulemaking. Example 5 shows that past processes do not count; only future participation does.
- **Subsection (a) is a unilateral power.** The Secretary may count certain patient days "to the extent... the Secretary determines appropriate." There is no requirement to act by regulation and no consultation, hearing or comment period.
- **No outside party is involved.** No state, expert or member of the public takes part in any coming federal decision.

qwen_chat.w: This section ratifies previously promulgated regulations and limits their application to closed cost reports. It does not require any new consultation, public hearing, comment period, or advisory committee involvement with parties outside the federal government. The act of ratification is an internal legal determination by Congress, not a participatory process involving the public or other external entities.
qwen_chat.s: (b) Ratification and Prospective Application of Previous Regulations.— (1) In general.—Subject to paragraph (2), regulations described in paragraph (3)... are hereby ratified, effective as of the date of their respective promulgations.
qwen_chat.b: Tempting-but-wrong reading: One might argue that because the section ratifies regulations, it implies a rulemaking process which typically involves public comment. However, the text itself only describes the legal effect of existing regulations (ratification) and does not mandate any new consultation, hearing, or comment period. The definition explicitly excludes "applications for benefits" and focuses on the *process* of participation. Ratifying a past rule is an internal legislative/executive act, not a participatory process with outsiders. Furthermore, the section does not grant a right to sue or require a new public hearing.
